title: View Through a Window May Influence Recovery from Surgery

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (deciduous trees)
findings.mechanism: Natural views elicit positive feelings, reduce fear, hold interest, and may block or reduce stressful thoughts, fostering restoration.
findings.quote: patients with window views of the trees spent less time in the hospital than those with views of the brick wall

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (deciduous trees)
findings.consequent: Number of negative evaluative comments in nurses' notes
findings.mechanism: Natural views elicit positive feelings, reduce fear, and foster restoration, leading to better emotional states.
findings.quote: More negative notes were made on patients with the brick wall view: 3.96 per patient compared to 1.13 per patient with the tree view

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (deciduous trees)
findings.consequent: Number of positive evaluative comments in nurses' notes
findings.quote: Although more positive comments were recorded for the tree-view patients, the difference was not statistically significant.

findings.antecedent: Window view (natural scene vs. brick wall)
findings.consequent: Analgesic doses (strong, moderate, weak) on Days 0-1 postoperative
findings.mechanism: Patients were too drugged or too absorbed by intense pain to attend to the windows.
findings.quote: In the other two periods there were no significant differ- ences.

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (deciduous trees)
findings.consequent: Overall analgesic doses (strong, moderate, weak) on Days 2-5 postoperative
findings.mechanism: Natural views foster restoration from anxiety or stress, potentially reducing pain perception or the need for potent analgesics.
findings.quote: For the period of primary interest, days 2 through 5, there were statistically significant variation between the tree-view and wall-view patients in the mean number of analgesic doses (T² = 13.52, F= 4.30, P < 0.01).

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (deciduous trees)
findings.consequent: Moderate and strong analgesic doses on Days 2-5 postoperative
findings.mechanism: Natural views foster restoration from anxiety or stress, potentially reducing pain perception or the need for potent analgesics.
findings.quote: In days 2 through 5 patients with the tree view took fewer moderate and strong pain doses than did the wall-view group

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (deciduous trees)
findings.consequent: Weak analgesic doses on Days 2-5 postoperative
findings.mechanism: Reduced need for strong analgesics due to restorative views leads to a shift towards weaker pain relief.
findings.quote: and more doses in the weak cate- gory. The wall group, therefore, was given many more doses of potent narcot- ics, whereas the tree group more fre- quently received such drugs as aspirin and acetaminophen.

findings.antecedent: Window view (natural scene vs. brick wall)
findings.consequent: Analgesic doses (strong, moderate, weak) on Days 6-7 postoperative
findings.mechanism: Only 45 percent of patients took any analgesics after the fifth day, indicating low overall need for pain medication.
findings.quote: In the other two periods there were no significant differ- ences.

findings.antecedent: Window view (natural scene vs. brick wall)
findings.mechanism: Wall-view patients were given more doses of narcotic analgesics, which produce drowsiness or sedation as side-effects, possibly reducing their need for sleeping pills or tranquilizers.
findings.quote: With respect to doses of antianxiety drugs, there was no significant variation between the groups.

findings.antecedent: Taking two or more strong or moderate analgesic doses
findings.mechanism: Narcotic analgesics produce drowsiness or sedation as side-effects, possibly reducing the need for sleeping pills or tranquilizers.
findings.quote: The observed frequency of doses was lower than the expected frequency when two or more strong or moderate analgesics were taken on the same day [x²(1) = 10.45, P < 0.01].

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (deciduous trees)
findings.mechanism: This small difference found may be due to the greater intake of potent analgesics by the wall-view group rather than to a possibly higher frequency of conversion reactions.
findings.quote: Although tree-view patients had lower scores, the difference was not statistical- ly significant.

stimuli.description: Window views of either a small stand of deciduous trees (natural scene) or a brown brick wall (monotonous built scene) from hospital rooms.

tables.description: Comparison of mean analgesic doses per patient for wall-view and tree-view groups across three time periods (Days 0-1, Days 2-5, Days 6-7) and three strength levels (Strong, Moderate, Weak).

limitations: The 'built' view in this study was a comparatively monotonous one, a largely featureless brick wall, so conclusions cannot be extended to all built views.
Conclusions cannot be extended to other patient groups, such as long-term patients, who may suffer from low arousal or boredom rather than from anxiety problems typically associated with surgeries.
